The core idea of SDQC is to decouple global observations into distinct reward-related and cost-related representations, aiming to improve generalization capabilities, particularly when faced with unfamiliar observations during testing. This decoupling is achieved through a Q-supervised contrastive learning approach, which encourages similar Q-values across actions to have similar representations, resulting in a coarser, yet theoretically sound, representation. The authors provide a theoretical foundation for their method, demonstrating that this coarser representation preserves the optimal policy while enhancing generalization. The method involves training separate representation networks for reward and cost, using a contrastive loss function that leverages the Q-function to identify similar and dissimilar states. These representations are then used to train three separate policies using weighted regressed diffusion models, an approach adapted from prior work. The empirical evaluation of SDQC is conducted on the DSRL benchmark, a standard suite for safe offline RL, and demonstrates that SDQC outperforms several baseline algorithms in terms of both safety and performance. Specifically, the results show that SDQC achieves near-zero constraint violations in many tasks and exhibits superior generalization in unseen environments.
